paragraphs: I was allowed to study abroad for three months at the University of Freiburg in Germany. I had wanted to go on the exchange program since I heard about it at an open campus event in the summer of my second year of high school, before entering Nagoya University, and I remember that I was both happy and felt my resolve tighten when I was able to take part. My motives for going abroad were vague ones, such as wanting to see European medicine, hoping it would be a reference for my future career, and somehow thinking it was cool, but after finishing the study abroad, having actually felt things on my skin, I gained more than that and it became a satisfying study abroad.

I was allowed to rotate for one month each through pediatric surgery, anesthesiology and radiology. In particular the first month, pediatric surgery, was a series of very fulfilling days. Monday, Wednesday and Friday were operating days and Tuesday and Thursday were outpatient days, and the operations I was able to see were mostly inguinal hernia and orchiopexy, but I also saw intestinal repairs such as for gastroschisis and meconium ileus. What I often saw on outpatient days was the examination of imperforate anus. A young doctor in his second year of becoming a pediatric surgeon taught me one-to-one. Since he had lived in the United States for 18 years, it was good that he taught me carefully in English. On operating days I was allowed to scrub into three operations every day, and when I said I wanted to do it, I was sometimes allowed to actually suture at the end when closing a patient. In particular, since I saw inguinal hernia operations more than 10 times, and because there were only four doctors, during vacation periods I was counted as part of the workforce, and there were more than three times when I took on operations as first assistant. Since I could borrow a suturing kit and practice actively in my free time, when I was told "better than the first closure!", I felt my own growth and also felt the time of having become a member of the team, and I was honestly happy.

During the three months in Germany I met various students and doctors. Through that I learned many things and gained many things that will serve as guidelines and nourishment in my career as a doctor from now on. Among them in particular, the mental strength to speak up on my own and deal with what was in front of me in an environment where only English was understood, and an earnest attitude by which I won trust even in a foreign land, are two things that could be gained only through this clerkship and that will be a mental support and confidence for me in my future career. Finally, I sincerely thank Dr. 粕谷, who gave me such a valuable experience, everyone at the International Exchange Office of Nagoya University School of Medicine, and everyone at the University of Freiburg who accepted me.
